resources.string: Accessibility-based device automation for MCP clients

DroidPilot Forge reads the on-screen content of other apps and performs taps, swipes and text input on your behalf. While the DroidPilot Forge server is running, these actions can be requested by an AI assistant on your local network that you have paired with this device using its pairing secret. Nothing is sent to the internet, and the server only runs while you have started it.
DroidPilot Forge needs this permission to read the screen and perform gestures. The server cannot run without it.
Restricts the server to this device. Use with “adb forward tcp:8765 tcp:8765” when you do not want it reachable over the network.
Your MCP client must present this secret to connect. It also encrypts the connection. Treat it like a password — anyone who has it can control this device while the server is running.
Every client paired with this device will stop working until you give it the new secret.
Enable the Accessibility service before starting the server.
Without notification permission, Android hides the DroidPilot Forge status notification — the server still runs, but you will not be able to see or stop it from the notification shade.
Shows while the DroidPilot Forge control server is accepting connections
Control server stopped after an error

Pairing a client lets it read the screen and tap. Running shell commands is a separate decision, and is denied until you grant it here. Grants apply to the currently paired client and end when you revoke them, when they expire, or when you regenerate the pairing secret.
No command access granted. Shell and root commands are refused.
Also allow the AI to initiate root
A root command can do anything on this device, including deleting data and changing system settings. Only grant this to a client you control.
This lets the AI decide, on its own, to run commands as root. It applies on top of root access, not instead of it — you must grant both.
Start the server once to create a pairing secret before granting access.
Changes what this screen shows and what the app reports to a connected client. Every command still requires the same authorisation as it does today — switching modes grants nothing.
"Tell me what to do on this device, and I\'ll do it." Direct commands, one at a time.
